p: Mr Gibbon began his history with the Roman Empire at the height of its prosperity, in the second century after Christ, and he was right to do so, for he wished to describe a fall, and a fall requires a height. My task is less elegant. I must begin at the bottom, in a darkness so ancient that the whole of written history, from the first clay tablets of Mesopotamia to the newspaper that Mrs Pruett has left upon my breakfast table, occupies less than one part in five hundred of it.

When I was a young man, it was the general opinion of educated Englishmen that the world had been created some six thousand years ago, and that mankind had appeared in it, fully formed and speaking, on the sixth day. Archbishop Ussher, a learned Irish prelate of the seventeenth century, had fixed the moment of creation, by careful arithmetic upon the generations of the Bible, at the year four thousand and four before Christ. That date was printed in the margins of a great many family Bibles, and a great many families believed it. It has not survived the century. The geologists, beginning with Mr James Hutton of Edinburgh and continuing with Sir Charles Lyell, whose Principles of Geology I read as an undergraduate with the guilty excitement of a boy reading a novel, showed that the rocks were laid down over spans of time beyond all easy reckoning. Then, in eighteen fifty-nine, Mr Charles Darwin published his book On the Origin of Species, and in eighteen seventy-one his Descent of Man, and the question of our own ancestry was opened to the light. It has not been closed since.
## What the Encyclopaedia of the future says

I shall tell you what the pages from the future report, and you will understand that in my own day much of it would have been called fantasy. The family of creatures to which we belong, the great apes, includes the chimpanzee, the gorilla and the orang-utan. Our own line and that of the chimpanzee are thought to have parted somewhere between six and seven million years ago, in Africa. The evidence is partly in the bones, which the patient diggers of the twentieth century found in remarkable numbers in the valleys and lake beds of eastern and southern Africa, and partly in a source I cannot pretend to understand: the inheritance carried within every living cell, which the men of the future have learned to read like a parish register, and which tells them how closely any two creatures are related.

Among the earliest of these ancestors that the diggers have named are creatures called the australopithecines, a word meaning the southern apes. They lived between about four million and two million years ago. They were small, with brains not much larger than a chimpanzee's, but they walked upright upon two legs. The most celebrated of them is a skeleton found in Ethiopia in nineteen seventy-four, which the finders named Lucy, after a popular song they were playing in their camp that evening. I mention this not to amuse you but because it is the kind of detail that historians of the future will treasure, as we treasure the fact that Archimedes ran naked from his bath.

Walking upright is a stranger achievement than it seems. It freed the hands. It allowed a creature to carry food, and children, across open country. It also made childbirth harder and the back more prone to complaint, as anyone who has bent to lift a heavy volume of Clarendon from a low shelf will confirm. Nature, like Parliament, rarely passes a reform without unintended consequences.

Some two to three million years ago appeared the first creatures that the learned place in our own genus, which they call Homo, the Latin word for man. Among the earliest is one called Homo habilis, meaning handy man, so named because its remains were found with simple stone tools. Then, from about two million years ago, came a larger and more capable creature called Homo erectus, meaning upright man. It was tall, long-legged, and built for walking great distances. It was the first of our relatives to leave Africa, spreading across Asia as far as China and the islands of Java, and it survived, in one form or another, for well over a million years: a dynasty that makes the Pharaohs look like a ministry that fell in a fortnight.

It is to these creatures, or to their near kin, that we owe the hand-axe and, very probably, the controlled use of fire, of which I shall speak separately. Their brains grew larger over the ages, though slowly, and the reasons for that growth are much argued. Some say it was the meat, others the cooking, others the need to remember the faces and quarrels of a large company of companions. I suspect that it was all of these, and I observe that the need to remember the quarrels of one's companions has not diminished.

Our own species, which the naturalists call Homo sapiens, meaning wise man, a title we have done much to deserve and more to forfeit, appeared in Africa some three hundred thousand years ago, if the Encyclopaedia is right; the oldest remains it mentions come from a place in Morocco called Jebel Irhoud. For a very long time our kind shared the world with others. In Europe and western Asia lived the Neanderthals, named after a valley in Germany where their bones were found in eighteen fifty-six, and which in my own day were thought by some to be the remains of a diseased Cossack. They were not. They were a people of great strength, who made fine tools, buried some of their dead, and survived the Ice Ages of Europe for hundreds of thousands of years. In Asia there were others, known chiefly from fragments, and on the island of Flores in the East Indies there lived, astonishingly, a race of very small people whom the diggers of the twenty-first century nicknamed the hobbits, after a children's book that I have not had the pleasure of reading.

Some time after about seventy thousand years ago, and perhaps earlier, our own kind spread out of Africa in large numbers and in the course of tens of thousands of years reached every habitable continent. Where they met the Neanderthals, they did not merely compete with them. The readers of the cellular register report that most people living today whose ancestors came from outside Africa carry a small portion of Neanderthal inheritance in their blood. That is to say, the two peoples, at least on occasion, married. The Neanderthals as a separate people vanished some forty thousand years ago. Whether by conquest, by disease, by the slow arithmetic of a slightly smaller birth rate, or by absorption into the newcomers, nobody can yet say, and I would not trust anybody who claimed to know.
## What all this means for the historian

You may ask why a historian of empires and laws should concern himself with bones. The answer is that every institution I shall describe in these lectures, every law, every creed, every engine, was built by creatures whose bodies and minds were shaped across these immense ages. We came into history already furnished with hands that could grasp a tool, voices that could form words, and a disposition, never yet cured, to live in groups, to love our own and to suspect the stranger. The study of our origins does not diminish mankind. It shows how much was achieved, by how many generations, before the first word was ever written.

There is one further lesson, and it is a humbling one. Through nearly the whole of this story, there were not one but several kinds of human being upon the earth. For the last few tens of thousands of years, there has been only one. We are the last survivors of a large and various family, and it would become us to be a little less proud of our pedigree and a little more careful of our inheritance.

The reading that follows, from the Encyclopaedia of the future, treats this subject at much greater length, and with many more names of species than I have troubled you with. If a name escapes you, let it go. The shape of the story is what matters: a long, slow, branching ascent, out of Africa and across the world.
